case_name: CASE OF ARVANITIS AND PHILELEFTHEROS PUBLIC COMPANY LIMITED v. CYPRUS

assessment.Existence of an interference: The applicants’ freedom of expression was interfered with when the domestic courts ordered them to pay EUR 12,000 in damages for defamation following the publication of an article criticizing lawyer C.K. (see paragraphs 8, 11, 15–16). This constitutes a clear interference with their Article 10 rights, as the judicial measure directly restricted their ability to express opinions on a matter of public interest.
assessment.Lawfulness of the interference: The interference had a legal basis under domestic law, specifically section 19 of the Civil Wrongs Law (Cap. 148), which governs defamation claims and provides for defences such as truth and fair comment (see paragraph 18). The national courts’ decisions were grounded in this statutory framework, fulfilling the requirement that the interference be prescribed by law under Article 10(2).
assessment.Legitimate aims of the interference: The interference pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the reputation of C.K., as recognized by the domestic courts. Under Article 10(2), the protection of the reputation or rights of others is a permissible ground for restricting freedom of expression. The national courts explicitly addressed the harm caused to C.K.’s personal and professional reputation due to the allegedly defamatory statements (see paragraphs 9, 12).
assessment.Necessary in a democratic society: The interference cannot be deemed necessary in a democratic society. While the national courts acknowledged the article addressed a matter of public interest—the recovery of Greek-Cypriot property from occupied territories (see paragraphs 6, 10, 13)—they failed to apply standards consistent with the ECtHR’s narrow margin for restrictions in public debates. C.K., as a lawyer actively engaged in high-profile litigation related to the Cyprus property issue and as the author of a widely published article, must be considered a limited-purpose public figure (see Morice v. France, no. 29369/10). The domestic courts incorrectly classified him as a private individual (see paragraphs 14, 16) and imposed an excessive burden of verification on the applicants. Furthermore, much of the article’s language (e.g., rhetorical questions and hyperbolic phrases in paragraph 6) constitutes value judgments protected under Article 10, even if phrased sharply (see Lingens v. Austria, no. 55480/00). The national courts’ strict interpretation of defamation law—requiring factual precision for opinion-based commentary and disregarding the public-interest context—undermines the robust debate essential in democratic societies (see Thorgeir Thorgeirson v. Iceland, no. 23556/94). Consequently, the interference was disproportionate.
